Both are the mendicant's rainy-season retreat undertaken so as not to harm beings on the roads; the rules and the festivals attached differ.
Both close or crown the rains with a communal act of reconciliation (Jain mutual forgiveness; Buddhist invitation to admonition); not the same rite.

Kundakunda's standpoint of ultimate reality plays the role of the ultimate level (P1) in relation to a conventional level used for teaching; it describes an individual pure soul and does not declare the world unreal, so only an analogy is asserted.
Both are the conventional level through which the ultimate is taught; the Jain standpoint remains a true partial view (naya), not an appearance.
Utt 23 itself explains Pārśva's and Mahāvīra's different rules by the capacities of each era's disciples — a text-internal instance of the stage-of-the-student principle.

Harikeśa's sacrifice of austerity re-reads the Vedic fire-offering as inner discipline, like the Āraṇyaka and Upaniṣadic internalizations; the Jain text rejects the outer sacrifice rather than subordinating it.
Both Jain passages ground brāhmaṇa-hood in conduct or vows; the Gītā's varṇa by guṇa and karma is a comparable move within the Vedic fold. Correspondence only, not identity.

Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma appear in the Jain universal history as baladevas and vāsudevas; the roles are recast (non-violent Rāma liberated, Lakṣmaṇa and Kṛṣṇa in hell), so this is a narrative correspondence, not an equivalence of doctrine.
